chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Uthman ibn Isa, from Sama'ah, who said:

I asked him (peace be upon him) about the man who comes to the mosque and its inhabitants have already prayed; should he begin with the prescribed prayer or offer optional prayers? So he (peace be upon him) said: If he is within a good time, there is no harm in offering optional prayers before the obligatory one; and if he fears missing out due to the passage of time, let him begin with the obligatory prayer, for it is the Right of Allah (Exalted and Majestic). Then let him offer optional prayers with whatever he desires.

Indeed, a person has leeway to pray the optional prayers at the beginning of the time of the obligatory prayer, unless he fears missing the obligatory one; and the superior manner, when a person prays alone, is to begin with the obligatory prayer when its time enters, so that the merit of the beginning of the time belongs to the obligatory prayer. And it is not forbidden upon him to pray the optional prayers from the beginning of the time until near the end of the time.
ai.seo_question: When should one pray optional prayers relative to the obligatory prayer?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi clarifies the juristic preference (tarjih) between offering voluntary prayers before the obligatory one, distinguishing between times of ease where both are permissible and times of urgency where the fard takes precedence to avoid missing its window. It highlights the Shia scholarly emphasis on securing the specific merit of 'first time' (awwal al-waqt) for the obligatory duty, particularly when praying individually, while maintaining that voluntary prayers are not prohibited until the very end of the time window. This ruling reflects the broader principle of balancing supererogatory devotion with the strict preservation of primary duties.
